subject: Science
title: Acids, Bases and Salts
summary: How acids and bases are identified with indicators, how they react with metals, carbonates, oxides and each other, what the pH scale measures and why it matters in the body and in soil, and how four industrial salts (sodium hydroxide, bleaching powder, baking soda, washing soda) plus plaster of Paris are made from common salt. It is one of the most equation-heavy chapters in Class 10 Science and a reliable source of 2- and 3-mark questions every year.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 10 Science is one 80-mark board paper. This chapter sits in the unit Chemical Substances: Nature and Behaviour, which carries about 25 marks across this unit's chapters. From this chapter alone you can typically expect 4 to 6 marks, spread over an MCQ or assertion-reason item, a 2- or 3-mark question on salts or pH, and occasionally a case-based passage.

question_types.note: Indicator colour changes, pH of everyday substances, which gas is evolved in a reaction, the formula of a named salt (CaOCl<sub>2</sub>, NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, CaSO<sub>4</sub>·½H<sub>2</sub>O), which salt is acidic or basic.
Acid added to water and not water to acid; dry HCl gas not changing litmus; plaster of Paris stored in a moisture-proof container; baking soda in cake mixtures.

Two uses of a salt with its formula; what happens when NaHCO<sub>3</sub> is heated (with equation); why distilled water does not conduct but rain water does; a labelled observation from a named activity.

Chlor-alkali process with products and uses; preparation and uses of bleaching powder, washing soda or plaster of Paris; pH in everyday life (tooth decay, bee sting, soil); reactions of acids with metals and carbonates with equations and the gas test.

Rare as a full 5-marker on its own. When it appears it is a combined question: a set of equations across acid, base, carbonate and oxide reactions, or the complete chlor-alkali story with the three products and one use each, or a comparison of baking soda, washing soda and bleaching powder.
A passage on pH of body fluids or soil, on antacids, on the HCl gas activity, or on the chlor-alkali process, followed by four sub-parts, one of which usually asks for an equation.

hot_topics: Chemicals from common salt: chlor-alkali process, bleaching powder, baking soda, washing soda (formula, preparation, uses)
Plaster of Paris and water of crystallisation (gypsum, CuSO<sub>4</sub>·5H<sub>2</sub>O)
pH scale and importance of pH in everyday life (tooth decay, antacids, bee sting, soil, acid rain)
Reaction of acids and bases with metals, and of acids with metal carbonates and hydrogencarbonates, with the gas tests
Why acids show acidic behaviour only in water: the dry HCl gas and litmus activity
Indicators: litmus, methyl orange, phenolphthalein, turmeric, olfactory indicators
Neutralisation, and the pH of salts formed from strong and weak acids and bases
Dilution of acids: why acid is added to water and what happens to H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> concentration

sections.heading: 2.1 Understanding the chemical properties of acids and bases: 2.1.1 Acids and bases in the laboratory
sections.body:
Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus red. Bases taste bitter, feel soapy and turn red litmus blue. In the lab you never taste anything, so you rely on indicators: substances whose colour (or smell) changes with the acidic or basic nature of the solution they are put in.

Litmus is the one NCERT starts with. It is a purple dye extracted from lichen, a plant of the Thallophyta group. In a neutral solution it stays purple; an acid turns it red and a base turns it blue. It is used either as a solution or as litmus paper (red and blue). Two synthetic indicators are also on the syllabus. Methyl orange is red in an acid and yellow in a base. Phenolphthalein is colourless in an acid and pink in a base. Learn these three colour pairs by heart; a one-mark question that gives a colour change and asks you to name the indicator or the solution turns up almost every year.

Natural indicators are found in coloured plant material: red cabbage leaves, the petals of the china rose (gudhal), and turmeric. China rose extract, normally light pink, turns magenta (dark pink) in an acid and green in a base. Turmeric is yellow and turns reddish-brown in a base, which is why a curry stain on a white shirt turns reddish-brown when soap (which is basic) is rubbed on it and goes back to yellow on rinsing with water.

An olfactory indicator is a substance whose smell changes in an acid or a base. Finely chopped onion, vanilla essence and clove oil are the NCERT examples: their smell is destroyed (cannot be detected) in a basic solution such as NaOH but remains in dilute HCl. So if you have unlabelled test tubes and are told to use only smell, onion-soaked cloth or vanilla essence lets you pick out the base.
sections.tip: If a question gives you three unlabelled solutions (acid, base, water) and only red litmus, the trick is: dip the paper in each; the one that turns it blue is the base. Now that blue paper, dipped in the remaining two, turns red only in the acid. The one left is water.

sections.heading: 2.1.2 How do acids and bases react with metals?
sections.body:
When a dilute acid reacts with an active metal, hydrogen gas is evolved and a salt is formed. The general form the examiner wants is: Acid + Metal → Salt + Hydrogen gas. Zinc granules with dilute sulphuric acid is the standard activity: bubbles of gas rise from the zinc, and when the gas is passed through soap solution the bubbles fill with hydrogen. Bring a burning candle near a gas-filled bubble and the gas burns with a pop sound. That pop is the test for hydrogen, and you should write it in every answer about acid-metal reactions.

Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2. The same thing happens with dilute HCl: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2. Note that the metal displaces hydrogen from the acid; the salt is named after the metal and the acid (zinc sulphate, zinc chloride).

Bases also react with some metals, and this is the part students forget. Zinc granules warmed with sodium hydroxide solution give hydrogen gas and sodium zincate: 2NaOH + Zn → Na2ZnO2 + H2. NCERT is careful to say that such reactions are not possible with all metals, so do not generalise to a rule that every base reacts with every metal. The general form is Base + Metal → Salt + Hydrogen gas, and when a question asks you to show that both acids and bases can liberate hydrogen with a metal, zinc is the metal to choose and the two equations above are the ones to write.

A useful lab detail: aluminium also gives hydrogen with NaOH (forming sodium aluminate), which is why aluminium vessels should not be used to store strong alkalis. That is beyond the NCERT text but it is a sensible reasoning point if a question asks about storage.

where: gas burns with a pop sound

sections.tip: Write the state of the gas as H<sub>2</sub>, never H. Losing the subscript is a common half-mark deduction on equation questions.

sections.heading: 2.1.3 How do metal carbonates and metal hydrogencarbonates react with acids?
sections.body:
Both a metal carbonate and a metal hydrogencarbonate react with an acid to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide. General form: Metal carbonate (or hydrogencarbonate) + Acid → Salt + Water + Carbon dioxide.

Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2, and NaHCO3 + HCl → NaCl + H2O + CO2. The same pattern holds for calcium carbonate (marble, egg shell, limestone): CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. This is the equation behind the NCERT in-text question where a metal compound A gives brisk effervescence with dilute HCl and one product is calcium chloride; A is calcium carbonate.

The test for carbon dioxide is that it turns lime water milky. Lime water is calcium hydroxide solution, and the milkiness is a white precipitate of calcium carbonate: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O. If you keep passing CO2 in excess, the milkiness disappears because the insoluble carbonate is converted into soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate: CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 → Ca(HCO3)2. Examiners like this two-step story: the milkiness appears, then clears. Give both equations.

Limestone, chalk and marble are all forms of calcium carbonate, which is why marble statues and buildings are damaged by acid rain. The gas evolved here is CO2, not hydrogen, so do not mention a pop sound in a carbonate question. That is one of the most common mix-ups in the answer scripts.

where: soluble, so the milkiness disappears with excess CO<sub>2</sub>

sections.tip: Distinguish the two gas tests clearly: hydrogen burns with a pop; carbon dioxide turns lime water milky. Mixing them up costs the whole mark for the test.

sections.heading: 2.1.4 How do acids and bases react with each other? (Neutralisation)
sections.body:
When an acid and a base react, each cancels the effect of the other; the reaction is called neutralisation and the products are a salt and water. Acid + Base → Salt + Water. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O is the equation every marking scheme accepts, and adding a second example such as KOH + HNO3 → KNO3 + H2O or Ca(OH)2 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + 2H2O earns the second example mark.

The NCERT activity uses phenolphthalein. A few drops are added to dilute NaOH: the solution turns pink. Dilute HCl is added drop by drop with stirring; the pink disappears when the base is exactly used up. Add NaOH again and the pink returns. Two things the examiner looks for in this activity answer: the colour goes pink with base and colourless with acid, and the colour change is reversible because it depends only on which of acid or base is present in excess.

Neutralisation is exothermic; that is why the beaker gets warm. In ionic terms the reaction is simply H+ + OH− → H2O, which will help you in section 2.2.

Everyday neutralisations you should be able to quote: an antacid such as milk of magnesia (magnesium hydroxide) neutralises excess HCl in the stomach; baking soda (mild base) rubbed on a bee sting neutralises the methanoic acid injected; lime (quicklime or slaked lime) or chalk added to acidic soil; a farmer may add organic matter to soil that has turned basic. The NCERT exercise Q3 is a proportion problem based on neutralisation: if 10 mL of NaOH solution is exactly neutralised by 8 mL of HCl, then 20 mL of the same NaOH needs 16 mL of that HCl.

where: the essential ionic change in every neutralisation

sections.tip: If asked to define neutralisation, write the general word equation and one balanced example, not just the definition. The definition alone is worth one mark; the example is the second.

sections.heading: 2.1.5 Reaction of metallic oxides with acids
sections.body:
A metal oxide reacts with an acid to give a salt and water, exactly as a base does. Because of this, metallic oxides are called basic oxides. The NCERT activity uses copper(II) oxide: a small amount of the black powder is added to dilute HCl and the mixture is stirred. The black solid dissolves and the solution turns bluish-green because copper(II) chloride is formed.

CuO + 2HCl → CuCl2 + H2O. General form: Metal oxide + Acid → Salt + Water. Other examples you can quote: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O and CaO + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O.

Why does this count as evidence that metal oxides are basic? Because the pattern (salt plus water with an acid) is the pattern of a base, and a base is by definition what neutralises an acid. In a reasoning question this is the sentence to write: metallic oxides give salt and water with acids, which is the characteristic property of bases, hence they are basic in nature.

Colour observations are commonly tested here. Copper(II) oxide is black; the copper(II) chloride solution is bluish-green. A question may describe the observation and ask you to identify the compound, or give the equation and ask for the colour change. Be precise: black solid to bluish-green solution.

where: black CuO dissolves, solution turns bluish-green

sections.tip: Metal oxide + acid → salt + water, but there is no gas evolved. Students sometimes write hydrogen here by analogy with metals; that is wrong.

sections.heading: 2.1.6 Reaction of a non-metallic oxide with base
sections.body:
Non-metallic oxides do the opposite of metallic oxides: they react with bases to give a salt and water, so they are acidic in nature. The NCERT example is carbon dioxide with calcium hydroxide (lime water): Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O. You have already met this as the lime-water test; here the point is what it tells you about CO2.

Because carbon dioxide reacts with a base the way an acid does, it behaves as an acidic oxide. Other non-metal oxides on the same side of the fence are sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide, which is why they dissolve in rain to make acid rain (rain water with pH less than 5.6). Sulphur dioxide with sodium hydroxide gives sodium sulphite and water: 2NaOH + SO2 → Na2SO3 + H2O. With carbon dioxide, sodium hydroxide gives sodium carbonate: 2NaOH + CO2 → Na2CO3 + H2O.

Put the two oxide sections side by side and you have a small table worth memorising: metallic oxides (CuO, MgO, CaO) are basic and react with acids; non-metallic oxides (CO2, SO2) are acidic and react with bases. Both reactions produce salt and water. This is the NCERT summary point and it is a favourite one-mark item phrased as: which of these oxides will react with NaOH?

NCERT returns to these acid-base properties of oxides in Chapter 3 (Metals and Non-metals), so expect an occasional cross-chapter question that gives an oxide and asks for its nature and one equation.

where: CO<sub>2</sub> acts as an acidic oxide

sections.tip: Metallic oxide → basic; non-metallic oxide → acidic. Write which one reacts with which before writing the equation.

sections.heading: 2.2 What do all acids and all bases have in common?
sections.body:
All acids contain hydrogen, but not every hydrogen-containing compound is an acid. The NCERT activity tests dilute HCl, dilute H2SO4, glucose solution and alcohol with a bulb-and-electrodes circuit: the bulb glows with the acids but not with glucose or alcohol. So acids produce ions in solution (they conduct), while glucose and alcohol, although they contain hydrogen, do not give H+ ions and are not acids.

The property common to all acids is that they produce hydrogen ions, H+(aq), in water. The property common to all bases is that they produce hydroxide ions, OH−(aq), in water. Bases that are soluble in water are called alkalis (NaOH, KOH); every alkali is a base but not every base is an alkali. NCERT's example of an insoluble base is copper oxide; magnesium hydroxide is only sparingly soluble.

The conduction activity is the standard answer to why an aqueous solution of an acid conducts electricity: the acid dissociates in water to give H+ ions (as H3O+) and anions, and these mobile ions carry the current. It is also the answer to NCERT exercise Q7: distilled water contains no ions and so does not conduct, while rain water has dissolved acidic gases (CO2, SO2) and other impurities that give ions, so it conducts.

The dry HCl activity is the most-asked experiment in the chapter. Dry HCl gas is prepared by heating a little sodium chloride with concentrated sulphuric acid: 2NaCl + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + 2HCl. The gas is dried by passing it through a guard tube containing calcium chloride. A dry blue litmus paper held in the gas shows no colour change; a moist blue litmus paper turns red. Conclusion: hydrogen ions are produced only in the presence of water; dry HCl gas contains no H+(aq), so it is not acidic. This is why NCERT says acids show acidic behaviour only in aqueous solution. The guard tube is there to keep the gas dry, and the question that asks you why the guard tube is used is really asking you to say exactly that.

where: preparation of dry HCl gas in the litmus activity

sections.tip: When you describe the dry HCl activity, mention all three: the gas is dried with a CaCl<sub>2</sub> guard tube, dry litmus shows no change, moist litmus turns red. Missing the moist litmus observation loses the concluding mark.

sections.heading: 2.2.1 What happens to an acid or a base in a water solution?
sections.body:
Hydrogen ions cannot exist alone in water; they attach to water molecules and exist as hydronium ions, H3O+. So the honest way to write the dissociation of HCl is HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl−, though H+(aq) is accepted as a shorthand. Bases dissociate to give hydroxide ions: NaOH(s) → Na+(aq) + OH−(aq); KOH(s) → K+(aq) + OH−(aq); Mg(OH)2(s) → Mg2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq).

Dissolving an acid or a base in water is highly exothermic. When concentrated acid is diluted, the acid must be added slowly to water with constant stirring. If water is added to concentrated acid instead, the heat released is so large that the mixture can boil locally and splash out of the container, and the glass may crack because of the sudden rise in temperature. This is the safety rule behind the warning label on concentrated acid bottles, and it is a routine assertion-reason item. Diluting a strong base also releases heat, so the same care is needed.

Dilution and ion concentration is the third idea here. Mixing an acid (or base) with water decreases the concentration of H3O+ (or OH−) ions per unit volume; the number of ions does not change, but the volume they are spread over increases. Diluting an acid therefore makes it weaker in effect and raises its pH toward 7. Adding more base to a base raises the OH− concentration per unit volume, though NCERT points out that beyond a point the increase is small because there is a limit to how much dissolves.

Two NCERT in-text questions come straight from here: why does dry HCl gas not change the colour of dry litmus (no water, so no H+ ions), and how does the concentration of hydronium ions change on dilution (it decreases). Learn to answer both in two sentences.

where: hydronium ion; H<sup>+</sup> cannot exist alone in water
the ion common to all bases in water

sections.tip: Say 'acid is added to water' and give both reasons: the process is exothermic, and adding water to acid can cause splashing and cracking of the container. One reason without the other is a half answer.

sections.heading: 2.3 How strong are acid or base solutions?
sections.body:
The pH scale measures the hydrogen ion concentration of a solution. The p comes from the German word potenz, meaning power. The scale runs from 0 (very acidic) to 14 (very alkaline). Neutral solutions have pH 7. A pH below 7 means an acidic solution; the lower the pH, the higher the H+ concentration and the stronger the acid. A pH above 7 means a basic solution; the higher the pH, the higher the OH− concentration and the stronger the base. pH is measured with universal indicator (a mixture of several indicators that shows a range of colours) or pH paper, and NCERT gives a colour chart to read the value off.

Strength depends on how completely the substance ionises in water. Strong acids (HCl, H2SO4, HNO3) give a high concentration of H+ ions; weak acids (acetic acid, formic acid, carbonic acid) give fewer H+ ions at the same concentration. Strong bases (NaOH, KOH) ionise fully; ammonium hydroxide is a weak base. That is why acetic acid of the same concentration as HCl has a higher pH, fizzes more slowly with magnesium ribbon (NCERT exercise Q10) and is called a weak acid.

Approximate pH values worth knowing (from the NCERT figure): 1 M HCl about 0, gastric juice about 1.2, lemon juice about 2.2, pure water 7, human blood about 7.4, milk of magnesia about 10, 1 M NaOH about 14. A question may list five solutions with pH values (as NCERT exercise Q9 does: A 4, B 1, C 11, D 7, E 9) and ask you to pick the most acidic (lowest pH, B) and the most basic (highest pH, C), then arrange them in increasing H+ concentration: C, E, D, A, B.

One more relation the examiner rewards: each unit decrease in pH means a ten-fold increase in H+ concentration. You are not asked to calculate with logarithms in Class 10, but you should know that pH 2 is ten times more acidic than pH 3, and you should be able to say that a solution of pH 6 has less hydrogen ion concentration than a solution of pH 2.

formulas.expr: pH < 7 acidic; pH = 7 neutral; pH > 7 basic

sections.tip: The most common trap: students write that higher pH means a stronger acid. It is the reverse. Lower pH = more H<sup>+</sup> = stronger acid.

sections.heading: 2.3.1 Importance of pH in everyday life
sections.body:
Living organisms are pH-sensitive. The human body works within a pH range of about 7.0 to 7.8, and most biochemical processes fail outside it. Rain with pH below 5.6 is acid rain; when it flows into rivers it lowers their pH, and aquatic life finds it hard to survive. Plants need a specific pH range of soil for healthy growth, so a farmer tests the soil and, if it is too acidic, adds quicklime (calcium oxide), slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) or chalk (calcium carbonate) to neutralise it. That is the answer to the NCERT in-text question about when a farmer would use lime.

Digestive system: the stomach produces hydrochloric acid that helps digest food without harming the stomach. When too much acid is produced there is pain and irritation (acidity), and the cure is an antacid, a mild base such as magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia) that neutralises the excess acid. Write the word neutralise; it is the marking point. This is also why NCERT exercise Q4 answers that indigestion is treated with an antacid.

Tooth decay: tooth enamel is made of calcium hydroxyapatite, a crystalline form of calcium phosphate, and is the hardest substance in the body. It does not dissolve in water but is corroded when the pH in the mouth falls below 5.5. Bacteria in the mouth produce acids by degrading sugar and food particles left after eating. The remedy is to clean the mouth after eating and to use toothpaste, which is generally basic, so that the excess acid is neutralised and decay is prevented.

Self defence by animals and plants: a bee sting leaves an acid (methanoic acid) that causes pain and irritation; rubbing a mild base such as baking soda on the stung area gives relief by neutralising it. The nettle plant has stinging hairs that inject methanoic acid; the traditional remedy is to rub the leaf of the dock plant, which often grows nearby. A case-based question on this section usually asks for the acid involved, the remedy and the name of the process (neutralisation) with one equation, so keep NaHCO3 + HCOOH → HCOONa + H2O + CO2 ready as an illustrative equation even though NCERT does not write it.
sections.tip: Three numbers to memorise in this section: acid rain pH below 5.6, tooth decay below pH 5.5, body works between pH 7.0 and 7.8.

sections.heading: 2.4 More about salts: 2.4.1 Family of salts and 2.4.2 pH of salts
sections.body:
A salt is the compound formed when an acid reacts with a base; it has a positive ion from the base and a negative ion from the acid. Salts with the same positive or negative radical belong to the same family. NaCl and Na2SO4 belong to the family of sodium salts; NaCl and KCl belong to the family of chloride salts. If a question lists a few salts and asks you to group them into families, look at the metal ion first, then the acid radical. Remember that potassium sulphate, sodium sulphate, calcium sulphate and magnesium sulphate all come from sulphuric acid, while sodium chloride and potassium chloride come from hydrochloric acid.

The pH of a salt depends on the strength of the acid and base it is made from. A salt of a strong acid and a strong base is neutral, pH 7 (NaCl from HCl and NaOH; K2SO4; NaNO3). A salt of a strong acid and a weak base is acidic, pH below 7 (NH4Cl from HCl and NH4OH; CuSO4). A salt of a weak acid and a strong base is basic, pH above 7 (Na2CO3 from carbonic acid and NaOH; CH3COONa from acetic acid and NaOH; NaHCO3). Sodium carbonate solution turning red litmus blue is the standard observation that shows a salt need not be neutral.

The NCERT activity has you dissolve NaCl, KNO3, Na2CO3, NH4Cl, NaHCO3, CH3COONa and similar salts and test them with litmus and pH paper, then write down the acid and base each one came from. A one-mark MCQ will show you a salt and ask whether its solution is acidic, basic or neutral; the rule above answers every such item.

Also note the colours and solubility facts that turn up: copper sulphate crystals are blue, sodium and potassium salts are generally white and soluble, and all the common salts in this chapter are ionic solids.
sections.tip: Strong + strong → neutral; strong acid + weak base → acidic; weak acid + strong base → basic. Write the parent acid and base next to each salt in your notes so the rule becomes automatic.

sections.heading: 2.4.3 Chemicals from common salt (I): common salt and the chlor-alkali process
sections.body:
Sodium chloride, common salt, is formed by the neutralisation of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide. It is dissolved in sea water along with other salts, and is obtained by evaporating sea water. Large solid deposits of it, called rock salt, formed when seas of earlier times dried up; rock salt is mined like coal and is often brown because of impurities. NCERT reminds you that common salt was the subject of Gandhiji's Dandi march. Common salt is the raw material for four important chemicals: sodium hydroxide, bleaching powder, baking soda and washing soda.

Sodium hydroxide is made by the chlor-alkali process: electrolysis of a concentrated aqueous solution of sodium chloride, called brine. The name comes from the products, chlor for chlorine and alkali for sodium hydroxide. 2NaCl(aq) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + Cl2(g) + H2(g). Chlorine gas is given off at the anode, hydrogen gas at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide solution is formed near the cathode. All three products are useful, and the marking scheme for a 3-mark question is usually one mark for the equation, one for the electrode at which each gas forms, and one for the uses.

Uses to quote. Hydrogen: fuels, margarine, ammonia for fertilisers. Chlorine: water treatment, swimming pools, PVC, disinfectants, CFCs, pesticides. Sodium hydroxide: degreasing metals, soaps and detergents, paper making, artificial fibres. Hydrogen and chlorine together give hydrochloric acid, used for cleaning steel, in ammonium chloride, medicines and cosmetics. Chlorine with slaked lime gives bleaching powder (next section).

Do not confuse this with the electrolysis of molten NaCl (which gives sodium metal and chlorine, and belongs to Chapter 3). In the chlor-alkali process the electrolyte is brine, an aqueous solution, and the product at the cathode is hydrogen, not sodium.
sections.tip: Write the three products with their electrodes: chlorine at anode, hydrogen at cathode, NaOH near cathode. Then one use each. That is the full 3-mark answer.

sections.heading: 2.4.3 Chemicals from common salt (II): bleaching powder and baking soda
sections.body:
Bleaching powder, CaOCl2 (calcium oxychloride), is produced by the action of chlorine on dry slaked lime: Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 → CaOCl2 + H2O. The chlorine comes from the chlor-alkali process, so the two topics are often examined together. Uses: bleaching cotton and linen in the textile industry, bleaching wood pulp in paper factories and washed clothes in the laundry; as an oxidising agent in many chemical industries; and for disinfecting drinking water to make it germ-free. The mild chlorine smell of bleaching powder is because it slowly releases chlorine in moist air, which is also why it should be stored dry.

Baking soda is sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO3. It is made from sodium chloride: NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 → NH4Cl + NaHCO3. It is a mild, non-corrosive base. On heating (or during baking) it decomposes: 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2. The carbon dioxide is what makes bread and cakes rise and become soft and spongy.

Baking powder is not the same as baking soda. Baking powder is a mixture of baking soda and a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid. When baking powder is heated or mixed in water, the acid reacts with the sodium hydrogencarbonate: NaHCO3 + H+ → CO2 + H2O + sodium salt of the acid. The tartaric acid has a second job: it neutralises the sodium carbonate formed, which would otherwise give the cake a bitter taste. A cake made with baking soda alone tastes bitter and rises less evenly; this is the CBSE 2019 reasoning question.

Uses of baking soda: an ingredient of baking powder; an antacid to neutralise excess stomach acid; and in soda-acid fire extinguishers, where its reaction with acid releases CO2 that smothers the fire. Adding a pinch of baking soda to milk slightly raises its pH so that the milk takes longer to set as curd (NCERT exercise Q12).

formulas.expr: NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub> + NH<sub>3</sub> → NH<sub>4</sub>Cl + NaHCO<sub>3</sub>

sections.tip: Three things are always asked about baking soda: its formula, what happens on heating (with equation), and why baking powder contains tartaric acid. Prepare all three as one answer.

sections.heading: 2.4.3 Chemicals from common salt (III): washing soda
sections.body:
Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3·10H2O. It is obtained from baking soda in two steps. First sodium hydrogencarbonate is heated to give sodium carbonate: 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2. Then the anhydrous sodium carbonate (soda ash) is recrystallised from water, taking up ten molecules of water of crystallisation: Na2CO3 + 10H2O → Na2CO3·10H2O. When a question asks how washing soda is prepared from baking soda, both equations are expected; the second is the one students skip.

Sodium carbonate is a basic salt (weak acid, strong base), so its solution turns red litmus blue and has pH above 7. The CBSE 2019 question that asked you to name the sodium compound that is basic and can be converted into washing soda wanted sodium hydrogencarbonate as the answer, with the two equations above.

Uses of washing soda: in glass, soap and paper industries; in the manufacture of sodium compounds such as borax; as a cleaning agent for domestic purposes; and for removing permanent hardness of water. The last use is the one asked most often. Hard water contains soluble calcium and magnesium salts (chlorides and sulphates); adding sodium carbonate precipitates them as insoluble carbonates, for example CaCl2 + Na2CO3 → CaCO3 + 2NaCl, so the water no longer forms scum with soap.

Keep the three sodium compounds separated in your head: NaHCO3 is baking soda; Na2CO3 (anhydrous) is soda ash; Na2CO3·10H2O is washing soda. A 2-mark difference question on baking soda versus washing soda wants formula, water of crystallisation (none versus ten) and one use each.
sections.tip: Washing soda is a hydrated salt: ten water molecules. Writing Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> alone as washing soda is marked wrong.

sections.heading: 2.4.4 Are the crystals of salts really dry? Water of crystallisation and plaster of Paris
sections.body:
Crystals of some salts look dry but contain a fixed number of water molecules as part of their crystal structure. This is water of crystallisation: the fixed number of water molecules present in one formula unit of a salt. Examples: copper sulphate pentahydrate CuSO4·5H2O (five), washing soda Na2CO3·10H2O (ten), gypsum CaSO4·2H2O (two).

The NCERT activity heats blue copper sulphate crystals in a dry boiling tube. Water droplets appear on the cooler walls of the tube and the crystals turn white (anhydrous copper sulphate). Adding two or three drops of water to the white powder brings the blue colour back. Both observations are tested: colour blue to white on heating (loss of water of crystallisation), and white to blue on adding water (water of crystallisation regained). CuSO4·5H2O ⇌ CuSO4 + 5H2O, forward on heating, backward on adding water.

Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO4·½H2O. It is prepared by heating gypsum at 373 K: CaSO4·2H2O →(373 K) CaSO4·½H2O + 1½H2O. The temperature matters; if gypsum is heated above 373 K it loses all its water and forms anhydrous calcium sulphate (dead burnt plaster), which does not set. The half molecule of water in the formula means two formula units of CaSO4 share one molecule of water.

Plaster of Paris is a white powder. Mixed with water it sets into a hard solid mass of gypsum within minutes: CaSO4·½H2O + 1½H2O → CaSO4·2H2O. That is why doctors use it to support fractured bones in the right position, and why it is used for making toys, materials for decoration and for making surfaces smooth. It must be stored in a moisture-proof container because even moisture from the air converts it into gypsum, after which it is useless as a plaster (NCERT exercise Q13).

where: setting of plaster of Paris into hard gypsum

sections.tip: Always give the temperature 373 K with the gypsum-to-plaster equation, and say what goes wrong above it. That detail separates a full-mark answer from a two-thirds one.

key_terms.definition: A substance that shows a change in colour (or smell) when added to an acidic or basic solution, and so tells you the nature of the solution. Litmus, methyl orange, phenolphthalein and turmeric are examples.
A substance whose smell changes in an acidic or basic medium. Onion, vanilla essence and clove oil lose their smell in a base.
A purple dye extracted from lichen (Thallophyta). It turns red in an acid and blue in a base; purple in a neutral solution.
A base that is soluble in water, such as NaOH and KOH. All alkalis are bases but not all bases are alkalis.
The reaction between an acid and a base in which each cancels the effect of the other, giving a salt and water. It is exothermic.
H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, formed when a hydrogen ion from an acid combines with a water molecule; H<sup>+</sup> cannot exist alone in water.
A scale from 0 to 14 for measuring hydrogen ion concentration. pH 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 basic. The p stands for potenz, German for power.
Strong acids (HCl, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, HNO<sub>3</sub>) ionise completely and give a high H<sup>+</sup> concentration; weak acids (acetic, formic, carbonic) ionise partially.
A mixture of several indicators that shows different colours at different pH values, so the pH of a solution can be read from a colour chart.
An ionic compound formed by the reaction of an acid with a base; it contains the positive ion of the base and the negative ion of the acid.
Salts having the same positive or the same negative radical, for example NaCl and Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (sodium salts) or NaCl and KCl (chlorides).
A concentrated aqueous solution of sodium chloride, the electrolyte in the chlor-alkali process.
Electrolysis of brine to give sodium hydroxide, chlorine (at the anode) and hydrogen (at the cathode).
Calcium oxychloride, CaOCl<sub>2</sub>, made by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime; used for bleaching, as an oxidising agent and for disinfecting water.
Sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, a mild non-corrosive base that gives CO<sub>2</sub> on heating; used in baking powder, antacids and fire extinguishers.
A mixture of baking soda and a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid; the acid releases CO<sub>2</sub> from the soda and neutralises the bitter sodium carbonate.

Sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>·10H<sub>2</sub>O, obtained by recrystallising sodium carbonate; used in glass, soap and paper industries and to remove permanent hardness of water.
The fixed number of water molecules present in one formula unit of a salt, e.g. five in CuSO<sub>4</sub>·5H<sub>2</sub>O and ten in Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>·10H<sub>2</sub>O.
Calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO<sub>4</sub>·½H<sub>2</sub>O, made by heating gypsum at 373 K; sets to hard gypsum on mixing with water.
Calcium sulphate dihydrate, CaSO<sub>4</sub>·2H<sub>2</sub>O, the raw material for plaster of Paris and the product formed when plaster sets.
A mild base such as magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia) taken to neutralise excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
Rain water with pH less than 5.6, caused by dissolved oxides such as SO<sub>2</sub> and NO<sub>2</sub>; it damages aquatic life and marble structures.

ncert_questions.q: You have been provided with three test tubes. One of them contains distilled water and the other two contain an acidic solution and a basic solution respectively. If you are given only red litmus paper, how will you identify the contents of each test tube?
ncert_questions.a:
Dip the red litmus paper into each of the three solutions in turn. The solution that turns the red litmus blue is the basic solution.

Now take this blue litmus paper (it has been turned blue by the base) and dip it into the remaining two test tubes. The solution that turns it red again is the acidic solution. The solution in which no colour change takes place is distilled water.

ncert_questions.q: Why should curd and sour substances not be kept in brass and copper vessels?
ncert_questions.a: Curd and other sour substances contain acids. When kept in brass or copper vessels the acid reacts with the metal, forming toxic salts (of copper) that dissolve into the food and make it unfit for eating. The vessel is also corroded.

ncert_questions.q: Which gas is usually liberated when an acid reacts with a metal? Illustrate with an example. How will you test for the presence of this gas?
ncert_questions.a:
Hydrogen gas is liberated. Example: zinc reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to give zinc sulphate and hydrogen: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2.

Test: pass the gas through soap solution to form gas-filled bubbles and bring a burning candle near them; hydrogen burns with a pop sound.

ncert_questions.q: Metal compound A reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce effervescence. The gas evolved extinguishes a burning candle. Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction if one of the compounds formed is calcium chloride.
ncert_questions.a:
A gas that extinguishes a burning candle and is given off with effervescence from a metal compound and dilute HCl is carbon dioxide. So A is a carbonate, and since calcium chloride is formed, A is calcium carbonate.

CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2

ncert_questions.q: Why do HCl, HNO<sub>3</sub> etc. show acidic characters in aqueous solutions while solutions of compounds like alcohol and glucose do not show acidic character?
ncert_questions.a: HCl and HNO3 dissociate in water to give hydrogen ions, H+(aq) (present as H3O+), and it is these ions that are responsible for acidic character: HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl−. Alcohol and glucose contain hydrogen, but they do not ionise in water to give H+ ions, so their solutions are not acidic. This is confirmed by the fact that their solutions do not conduct electricity while acid solutions do.

ncert_questions.q: Why does dry HCl gas not change the colour of the dry litmus paper?
ncert_questions.a: Dry HCl gas contains no water, so it does not dissociate into H+(aq) ions. Acidic character is due to H+ ions produced only in the presence of water. In the absence of these ions the dry gas cannot turn dry blue litmus red. (If the litmus paper is moist, the HCl dissolves in the moisture, forms H+ ions, and the paper turns red.)

ncert_questions.q: While diluting an acid, why is it recommended that the acid should be added to water and not water to the acid?
ncert_questions.a: Dissolving an acid in water is a highly exothermic process. If water is added to concentrated acid, the large amount of heat released can make the mixture boil locally and splash out, causing burns, and the sudden rise in temperature can crack the glass container. When acid is added slowly to a larger volume of water with stirring, the heat is absorbed by the water and dissipated safely.

ncert_questions.q: Under what soil condition do you think a farmer would treat the soil of his fields with quick lime (calcium oxide) or slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) or chalk (calcium carbonate)?
ncert_questions.a: When the soil is too acidic (pH well below the range plants need), the farmer adds quicklime, slaked lime or chalk. These are basic substances that neutralise the excess acid in the soil and bring its pH toward the range suitable for healthy plant growth.

ncert_questions.q: What will happen if a solution of sodium hydrogencarbonate is heated? Give the equation of the reaction involved.
ncert_questions.a: On heating, sodium hydrogencarbonate decomposes to give sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide: 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2. The carbon dioxide escapes as a gas and the solution left contains sodium carbonate.

ncert_questions.q: A solution turns red litmus blue; its pH is likely to be (a) 1 (b) 4 (c) 5 (d) 10
ncert_questions.a: (d) 10. A solution that turns red litmus blue is basic, and a basic solution has pH greater than 7. The only option above 7 is 10.

ncert_questions.q: A solution reacts with crushed egg-shells to give a gas that turns lime-water milky. The solution contains (a) NaCl (b) HCl (c) LiCl (d) KCl
ncert_questions.a: (b) HCl. Egg shells are calcium carbonate. A gas that turns lime water milky is CO2, which a carbonate gives only with an acid: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. NaCl, LiCl and KCl are neutral salts and do not react.

ncert_questions.q: 10 mL of a solution of NaOH is found to be completely neutralised by 8 mL of a given solution of HCl. If we take 20 mL of the same solution of NaOH, the amount of HCl solution (the same solution as before) required to neutralise it will be (a) 4 mL (b) 8 mL (c) 12 mL (d) 16 mL
ncert_questions.a: (d) 16 mL. The volume of acid needed is directly proportional to the volume of the same base. 10 mL NaOH needs 8 mL HCl, so 20 mL NaOH (twice as much) needs 2 × 8 = 16 mL HCl.

ncert_questions.q: Which one of the following types of medicines is used for treating indigestion? (a) Antibiotic (b) Analgesic (c) Antacid (d) Antiseptic
ncert_questions.a: (c) Antacid. Indigestion is caused by excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach; an antacid is a mild base (for example magnesium hydroxide) that neutralises the excess acid.

ncert_questions.q: Write word equations and then balanced equations for the reaction taking place when (a) dilute sulphuric acid reacts with zinc granules (b) dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with magnesium ribbon (c) dilute sulphuric acid reacts with aluminium powder (d) dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with iron filings.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Zinc + dilute sulphuric acid → zinc sulphate + hydrogen; Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2

(b) Magnesium + dilute hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen; Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2

(c) Aluminium + dilute sulphuric acid → aluminium sulphate + hydrogen; 2Al + 3H2SO4 → Al2(SO4)3 + 3H2

(d) Iron + dilute hydrochloric acid → iron(II) chloride + hydrogen; Fe + 2HCl → FeCl2 + H2

ncert_questions.q: Compounds such as alcohols and glucose also contain hydrogen but are not categorised as acids. Describe an activity to prove it.
ncert_questions.a:
Take dilute HCl, dilute H2SO4, glucose solution and alcohol in separate beakers. Fix two nails on a cork in each beaker and connect the nails to the two terminals of a battery through a bulb and a switch. Switch on the current. The bulb glows in the acid solutions but does not glow in glucose solution or alcohol.

Conclusion: the acids dissociate in water to give ions (H+ and anions) that conduct electricity; glucose and alcohol do not ionise and give no H+ ions, so they are not acids even though they contain hydrogen.

ncert_questions.q: Why does distilled water not conduct electricity, whereas rain water does?
ncert_questions.a: Distilled water is pure and contains almost no ions, so there is nothing to carry the current. Rain water dissolves acidic gases from the air (such as CO2 and SO2) forming carbonic and other acids, and also picks up dissolved salts and dust. These provide ions, so rain water conducts electricity.

ncert_questions.q: Why do acids not show acidic behaviour in the absence of water?
ncert_questions.a: The acidic behaviour of an acid is due to the hydrogen ions, H+(aq), it produces. An acid dissociates to give these ions only when it is dissolved in water, because water molecules are needed to form hydronium ions, H3O+. In the absence of water there is no dissociation and no H+ ions, so the acidic properties (turning litmus red, and so on) are not shown; for example dry HCl gas does not change the colour of dry blue litmus.

ncert_questions.q: Five solutions A, B, C, D and E when tested with universal indicator showed pH as 4, 1, 11, 7 and 9 respectively. Which solution is (a) neutral (b) strongly alkaline (c) strongly acidic (d) weakly acidic (e) weakly alkaline? Arrange the pH in increasing order of hydrogen-ion concentration.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Neutral: D (pH 7). (b) Strongly alkaline: C (pH 11). (c) Strongly acidic: B (pH 1). (d) Weakly acidic: A (pH 4). (e) Weakly alkaline: E (pH 9).

Hydrogen-ion concentration increases as pH decreases, so in increasing order of H+ concentration: C (11) < E (9) < D (7) < A (4) < B (1), i.e. 11 < 9 < 7 < 4 < 1.

ncert_questions.q: Equal lengths of magnesium ribbons are taken in test tubes A and B. Hydrochloric acid is added to test tube A, while acetic acid is added to test tube B. Amount and concentration taken for both the acids are the same. In which test tube will the fizzing occur more vigorously and why?
ncert_questions.a: Fizzing will be more vigorous in test tube A (hydrochloric acid). HCl is a strong acid that dissociates completely in water and gives a higher concentration of H+ ions than acetic acid, which is a weak acid and dissociates only partially. More H+ ions means hydrogen gas is evolved faster: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2.

ncert_questions.q: Fresh milk has a pH of 6. How do you think the pH will change as it turns into curd? Explain your answer.
ncert_questions.a: The pH will decrease (become less than 6). When milk turns into curd, bacteria convert the lactose in milk into lactic acid. The acid formed increases the hydrogen-ion concentration, so the pH falls and the curd tastes sour.

ncert_questions.q: A milkman adds a very small amount of baking soda to fresh milk. (a) Why does he shift the pH of the fresh milk from 6 to slightly alkaline? (b) Why does this milk take a long time to set as curd?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Baking soda is a mild base. Making the milk slightly alkaline prevents it from turning sour easily, because the acid produced by bacteria is neutralised, so the milk keeps for longer.

(b) For milk to set as curd, enough lactic acid must form to lower the pH. In alkaline milk the lactic acid produced is first used up in neutralising the base, so it takes much longer for the pH to fall and for curd to form.

ncert_questions.q: Plaster of Paris should be stored in a moisture-proof container. Explain why?
ncert_questions.a: Plaster of Paris (CaSO4·½H2O) reacts with water, even the moisture in air, and sets into a hard solid mass of gypsum: CaSO4·½H2O + 1½H2O → CaSO4·2H2O. Once this happens it can no longer be mixed and used as plaster. So it is stored in a moisture-proof container to keep it from absorbing moisture.

ncert_questions.q: What is a neutralisation reaction? Give two examples.
ncert_questions.a:
The reaction of an acid with a base to form a salt and water, in which each cancels the effect of the other, is called a neutralisation reaction. Acid + Base → Salt + Water.

Examples: (i) NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O; (ii) Ca(OH)2 + H2SO4 → CaSO4 + 2H2O. Everyday examples: an antacid neutralising stomach acid; baking soda neutralising the acid of a bee sting.

ncert_questions.q: Give two important uses of washing soda and baking soda.
ncert_questions.a:
Washing soda (Na2CO3·10H2O): (i) used in glass, soap and paper industries; (ii) used for removing permanent hardness of water (also as a domestic cleaning agent).

Baking soda (NaHCO3): (i) an ingredient of baking powder, which makes cakes and bread soft and spongy; (ii) an antacid to neutralise excess acid in the stomach (also used in soda-acid fire extinguishers).

pyq.q: Which of the following indicators is colourless in an acidic solution and pink in a basic solution?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base. Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base; litmus is red/blue; turmeric is yellow/reddish-brown.

pyq.q: A gas is evolved when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to sodium hydrogencarbonate. The gas
options: has a pungent smell and turns moist blue litmus red
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: NaHCO<sub>3</sub> + HCl → NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub>; carbon dioxide turns lime water milky. Hydrogen is the gas that burns with a pop, and oxygen relights a splint.

pyq.q: Which of the following salts has no water of crystallisation?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Baking soda is NaHCO<sub>3</sub> with no water of crystallisation. Blue vitriol has five, washing soda ten and gypsum two water molecules per formula unit.

pyq.q: The pH of solutions P, Q, R and S is 2, 9, 7 and 12 respectively. Which solution has the highest hydroxide ion concentration?
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: OH<sup>−</sup> concentration increases with pH. S at pH 12 is the most basic and has the highest hydroxide ion concentration.

pyq.q: Which of the following is formed when chlorine is passed over dry slaked lime?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CaOCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O. Bleaching powder is calcium oxychloride.

pyq.q: In the chlor-alkali process, the gases evolved at the anode and cathode respectively are
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Electrolysis of brine gives chlorine at the anode and hydrogen at the cathode; sodium hydroxide forms near the cathode.

pyq.q: Which of the following salts, when dissolved in water, gives a solution with pH greater than 7?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Sodium carbonate is the salt of a weak acid (carbonic acid) and a strong base (NaOH), so its solution is basic. NaCl and KNO<sub>3</sub> are neutral; NH<sub>4</sub>Cl is acidic.

pyq.q: Tooth enamel starts corroding when the pH in the mouth falls below
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: NCERT states that tooth enamel (calcium hydroxyapatite) is corroded when the pH in the mouth falls below 5.5.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): While diluting a concentrated acid, the acid should be added slowly to water and not water to the acid. Reason (R): The dissolution of an acid in water is a highly exothermic process.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The process is highly exothermic; adding water to acid releases heat so fast that the mixture can splash out and the container may crack. So R correctly explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Dry HCl gas does not change the colour of dry blue litmus paper. Reason (R): HCl gas is a covalent compound and does not dissociate into ions in the absence of water.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Acidic character needs H<sup>+</sup>(aq) ions, which form only when HCl dissolves in water. Dry gas gives no ions, so no colour change. R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Plaster of Paris is stored in a moisture-proof container. Reason (R): Plaster of Paris is prepared by heating gypsum above 373 K.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: A is true: moisture converts plaster of Paris into hard gypsum. R is false: gypsum is heated at 373 K, not above it; above 373 K all the water is lost and dead burnt plaster forms.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Sodium carbonate solution is basic in nature. Reason (R): Sodium carbonate is a salt of a strong acid and a strong base.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> solution is basic (A true), but it is the salt of a weak acid (carbonic acid) and a strong base (NaOH), so R is false.

pyq.q: What is meant by water of crystallisation of a substance? Describe an activity to show that copper sulphate crystals contain water of crystallisation.
pyq.answer:
Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules present in one formula unit of a salt, for example five in CuSO4·5H2O.

Activity: heat a few blue copper sulphate crystals in a dry boiling tube. The crystals turn white and drops of water appear on the inner walls of the tube, showing that water was present in the crystals. On adding two or three drops of water to the white powder, the blue colour returns. CuSO4·5H2O ⇌ CuSO4 + 5H2O.

pyq.q: Name the sodium compound which is basic in nature and is used for making baking powder. How is it converted into washing soda? Write the equations involved.
pyq.answer:
Sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO3 (baking soda).

Conversion: on heating it gives sodium carbonate, 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2; the sodium carbonate is then recrystallised from water to give washing soda, Na2CO3 + 10H2O → Na2CO3·10H2O.

pyq.q: A few drops of phenolphthalein were added to a solution of sodium hydroxide, and then dilute hydrochloric acid was added drop by drop. What colour changes are observed and why? What happens if a few drops of NaOH are now added to this mixture?
pyq.answer:
On adding phenolphthalein to NaOH the solution turns pink, because phenolphthalein is pink in a basic medium. As dilute HCl is added drop by drop, the acid neutralises the base (NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O); when all the base has been used up the pink colour disappears and the solution becomes colourless.

If NaOH is added again, the solution becomes basic once more and the pink colour reappears.

pyq.q: Why does an aqueous solution of an acid conduct electricity? Name the ions responsible.
pyq.answer: An acid dissociates in water to form ions: hydrogen ions (present as hydronium ions, H3O+) and the corresponding anions, for example HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl−. These free, mobile ions carry the electric current through the solution, so a bulb connected across electrodes dipped in the acid solution glows. The ions responsible are H+/H3O+ and Cl− (for HCl).

pyq.q: During the preparation of a cake, a student used baking soda instead of baking powder. What would be the effect on the taste of the cake and why? What is the composition of baking powder?
pyq.answer:
The cake would taste bitter. On heating, baking soda decomposes to give sodium carbonate (2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2), and the sodium carbonate left in the cake is bitter.

Baking powder is a mixture of baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate) and a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid. The acid neutralises the sodium carbonate formed, so the cake does not taste bitter, and it also helps release CO2 which makes the cake rise.

pyq.q: What is the chlor-alkali process? Write the chemical equation and name the products formed at each electrode. Give one use of each product.
pyq.answer:
The chlor-alkali process is the electrolysis of an aqueous solution of sodium chloride (brine). Its name comes from the products: chlor for chlorine and alkali for sodium hydroxide.

2NaCl(aq) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + Cl2(g) + H2(g)

Chlorine is evolved at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide solution is formed near the cathode.

Uses: chlorine for water treatment and making PVC and bleaching powder; hydrogen as a fuel and for making ammonia for fertilisers and margarine; sodium hydroxide for making soaps and detergents, paper and artificial fibres, and for degreasing metals.

pyq.q: Describe with the help of a labelled diagram an activity to show that dry HCl gas does not turn dry blue litmus red but moist litmus does. What conclusion do you draw?
pyq.answer:
Take about 1 g of solid sodium chloride in a clean dry test tube and set up the apparatus with a delivery tube. Add concentrated sulphuric acid: 2NaCl + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + 2HCl. Pass the gas evolved through a guard tube containing calcium chloride so that the HCl gas is dry.

Hold a dry blue litmus paper at the mouth of the delivery tube: no colour change. Now hold a moist blue litmus paper: it turns red.

Conclusion: acidic character is due to H+(aq) ions, which are produced only when HCl dissolves in water. Dry HCl gas contains no H+ ions and so shows no acidic property; in the moist paper the gas dissolves, ionises and turns the litmus red. (Diagram: flask with NaCl and conc. H2SO4, delivery tube, calcium chloride guard tube, dry and moist litmus papers labelled.)

pyq.q: Write the chemical formula of bleaching powder. How is it prepared? Write the chemical equation and state any two uses.
pyq.answer:
Bleaching powder is calcium oxychloride, CaOCl2.

Preparation: chlorine gas (obtained from the chlor-alkali process) is passed over dry slaked lime. Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 → CaOCl2 + H2O.

Uses: (i) bleaching cotton and linen in the textile industry, wood pulp in paper factories and washed clothes in laundry; (ii) disinfecting drinking water to make it germ-free; (iii) as an oxidising agent in chemical industries.

pyq.q: What is plaster of Paris? Write its chemical formula and the equation for its preparation. Why is it called a hemihydrate? Give two uses.
pyq.answer:
Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO4·½H2O, a white powder obtained by heating gypsum at 373 K: CaSO4·2H2O →(373 K) CaSO4·½H2O + 1½H2O.

It is called a hemihydrate because it contains half a molecule of water of crystallisation per formula unit; two formula units of CaSO4 share one molecule of water.

Uses: doctors use it as plaster for supporting fractured bones in the right position; it is used for making toys, materials for decoration and for making surfaces smooth. On mixing with water it sets to hard gypsum: CaSO4·½H2O + 1½H2O → CaSO4·2H2O.

pyq.q: Give reasons: (a) A bee sting is treated by rubbing baking soda on the stung area. (b) A farmer adds lime to acidic soil. (c) Toothpaste is generally basic.
pyq.answer:
(a) A bee sting injects an acid (methanoic acid) that causes pain. Baking soda is a mild base and neutralises this acid, giving relief.

(b) Plants need soil of a particular pH range. When the soil is too acidic, lime (calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide) neutralises the excess acid and brings the pH into the suitable range.

(c) Bacteria in the mouth produce acids from the sugar and food particles left after eating. When the pH falls below 5.5 tooth enamel (calcium hydroxyapatite) is corroded. Toothpaste, being basic, neutralises the excess acid and prevents tooth decay.

pyq.q: How is washing soda prepared from sodium chloride? Write the equations. Why is it used for removing permanent hardness of water?
pyq.answer:
Step 1: sodium hydrogencarbonate is made from brine, NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 → NH4Cl + NaHCO3.

Step 2: heating gives sodium carbonate, 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2.

Step 3: recrystallisation gives washing soda, Na2CO3 + 10H2O → Na2CO3·10H2O.

Permanent hardness is due to dissolved chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium. Sodium carbonate removes these ions as insoluble carbonates, for example CaCl2 + Na2CO3 → CaCO3 + 2NaCl, so the water becomes soft.

pyq.q: (a) Write balanced chemical equations for the reaction of dilute hydrochloric acid with (i) zinc, (ii) sodium carbonate, (iii) copper(II) oxide. (b) Name the gas evolved in (i) and (ii) and give the test for each. (c) What is observed in (iii)?
pyq.answer:
(a) (i) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2; (ii) Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2; (iii) CuO + 2HCl → CuCl2 + H2O.

(b) In (i) hydrogen is evolved. Test: bring a burning candle or splint near the gas; it burns with a pop sound. In (ii) carbon dioxide is evolved. Test: pass the gas through lime water; the lime water turns milky, Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O.

(c) The black copper(II) oxide dissolves and the solution turns bluish-green because copper(II) chloride is formed. No gas is evolved; this shows that metallic oxides are basic in nature, since they give salt and water with an acid.

pyq.q: (a) What are strong and weak acids? Give one example of each. (b) Why is HCl a stronger acid than acetic acid of the same concentration? Which will have the lower pH? (c) Explain what happens to the pH and to the concentration of H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> ions when an acid is diluted. (d) State the precaution to be taken while diluting a concentrated acid.
pyq.answer:
(a) Strong acids ionise completely in water and give a large number of H+ ions, for example HCl, H2SO4, HNO3. Weak acids ionise only partially and give fewer H+ ions, for example acetic acid, formic acid, carbonic acid.

(b) HCl dissociates fully into H+ and Cl− whereas acetic acid dissociates only to a small extent, so HCl of the same concentration has a much higher H+ concentration. Since lower pH means higher H+ concentration, HCl has the lower pH.

(c) On dilution the same number of H3O+ ions is spread through a larger volume, so the concentration of H3O+ ions per unit volume decreases and the pH rises toward 7.

(d) The concentrated acid must be added slowly to water with constant stirring, never water to the acid, because the process is highly exothermic and adding water to acid can cause the mixture to splash out and the container to crack.

pyq.q: Compare baking soda, washing soda and bleaching powder under the heads: chemical name, formula, method of preparation (with equation) and one use each.
pyq.answer:
Baking soda: sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO3. Prepared from brine: NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 → NH4Cl + NaHCO3. Use: ingredient of baking powder; antacid.

Washing soda: sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3·10H2O. Prepared by heating baking soda, 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2, then recrystallising, Na2CO3 + 10H2O → Na2CO3·10H2O. Use: removing permanent hardness of water; glass, soap and paper industries.

Bleaching powder: calcium oxychloride, CaOCl2. Prepared by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime, Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 → CaOCl2 + H2O. Use: bleaching cotton and linen in textiles; disinfecting drinking water.

All three are ultimately obtained from common salt: NaHCO3 and Na2CO3·10H2O directly from brine, and CaOCl2 from the chlorine produced in the chlor-alkali process.

pyq.q:
The stomach produces hydrochloric acid, which helps digest food without harming the stomach. During indigestion the stomach produces too much acid, causing pain and irritation. A doctor may prescribe an antacid such as milk of magnesia. Similarly, tooth enamel, made of calcium hydroxyapatite, is the hardest substance in the body but is corroded when the pH in the mouth falls below 5.5. Bacteria in the mouth produce acid from food particles left after eating.
(i) Name the base present in milk of magnesia and write the equation for its reaction with stomach acid.
(ii) Why is toothpaste basic?
(iii) A student measured the pH of the mouth as 5.2 after a sugary snack. What does this indicate?
(iv) Which of the following has the lowest pH: gastric juice, saliva, blood?
pyq.answer:
(i) Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2. Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl → MgCl2 + 2H2O (neutralisation of excess acid).

(ii) Toothpaste is basic so that it neutralises the excess acid produced by bacteria in the mouth, keeping the pH above 5.5 and preventing corrosion of tooth enamel.

(iii) A pH of 5.2 is below 5.5, so acid produced from the sugar has made the mouth acidic enough to corrode enamel; the student should rinse the mouth or brush with toothpaste.

(iv) Gastric juice (pH about 1.2) has the lowest pH; blood is about 7.4 and saliva is close to neutral.

pyq.q:
Common salt is the raw material for several chemicals. When electricity is passed through a concentrated solution of sodium chloride (brine), it decomposes to form sodium hydroxide and two gases. One of the gases is passed over dry slaked lime to make a compound used for disinfecting drinking water. Another product is used to make soaps and detergents.
(i) Write the balanced equation for the electrolysis of brine and name the process.
(ii) Which gas is evolved at the anode and which at the cathode?
(iii) Name the compound formed with dry slaked lime and write its formula.
(iv) Name the product used for making soaps, and give one more use of it.
pyq.answer:
(i) 2NaCl(aq) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + Cl2(g) + H2(g); this is the chlor-alkali process.

(ii) Chlorine at the anode; hydrogen at the cathode.

(iii) Bleaching powder, calcium oxychloride, CaOCl2: Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 → CaOCl2 + H2O.

(iv) Sodium hydroxide. Other uses: degreasing metals, paper making, artificial fibres.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is an olfactory indicator?
practice_mcq.explanation: An olfactory indicator changes its smell in acid or base. Onion, vanilla essence and clove oil are the NCERT examples; the others are colour indicators.

practice_mcq.q: Turmeric stain on a white shirt turns reddish-brown when soap is applied because
practice_mcq.explanation: Turmeric is yellow in acid or neutral solution and reddish-brown in a base. Soap solution is basic.

practice_mcq.q: The gas evolved when zinc granules react with dilute sulphuric acid is
practice_mcq.explanation: Zn + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → ZnSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>; the hydrogen burns with a pop sound.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is formed when zinc reacts with sodium hydroxide?
practice_mcq.explanation: 2NaOH + Zn → Na<sub>2</sub>ZnO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>. Zinc is one of the metals that liberates hydrogen with a base too.

practice_mcq.q: When excess carbon dioxide is passed through lime water, the milkiness disappears because of the formation of
practice_mcq.explanation: CaCO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub> → Ca(HCO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, which is soluble in water, so the white precipitate dissolves.

practice_mcq.q: Copper(II) oxide reacts with dilute HCl to give a solution that is
practice_mcq.explanation: CuO + 2HCl → CuCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O; copper(II) chloride solution is bluish-green.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is an acidic oxide?
practice_mcq.explanation: Non-metallic oxides such as CO<sub>2</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub> react with bases to give salt and water, so they are acidic. The metal oxides are basic.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following solutions will make a bulb glow when tested with electrodes?
practice_mcq.explanation: Only the acid dissociates into ions (H<sup>+</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>), which conduct. Glucose and alcohol do not ionise; distilled water has almost no ions.

practice_mcq.q: The ion that cannot exist alone in water and combines with a water molecule is
practice_mcq.explanation: H<sup>+</sup> combines with H<sub>2</sub>O to form the hydronium ion, H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following statements about diluting an acid is correct?
options: Water should be added to concentrated acid slowly
The concentration of H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> ions per unit volume decreases
The pH of the acid decreases
practice_mcq.explanation: Dilution spreads the same ions over a larger volume, so H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> concentration decreases and pH rises. Acid is added to water; the process is exothermic.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following has the highest hydrogen ion concentration?
practice_mcq.explanation: The lower the pH, the higher the H<sup>+</sup> concentration. Lemon juice at pH 2.2 is the most acidic of the four.

practice_mcq.q: Rain is called acid rain when its pH is less than
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT defines acid rain as rain water with pH less than 5.6.

practice_mcq.q: A bee sting can be relieved by applying
practice_mcq.explanation: The sting injects methanoic acid; baking soda is a mild base that neutralises it. Vinegar and lemon juice are acids and would not help.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following salts is acidic in aqueous solution?
practice_mcq.explanation: NH<sub>4</sub>Cl is the salt of a strong acid (HCl) and a weak base (NH<sub>4</sub>OH), so its solution is acidic. The others are neutral or basic.

practice_mcq.q: Rock salt deposits were formed by
options: drying up of seas in earlier times
neutralisation of HCl by NaOH in mines
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT explains that large deposits of solid salt, rock salt, formed when seas of earlier times dried up; it is mined like coal.

practice_mcq.q: The chemical formula of baking soda is
practice_mcq.explanation: Baking soda is sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO<sub>3</sub>. Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>·10H<sub>2</sub>O is washing soda.

practice_mcq.q: Baking powder contains, besides baking soda,
options: a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid
practice_mcq.explanation: The tartaric acid releases CO<sub>2</sub> from NaHCO<sub>3</sub> on heating and neutralises the bitter sodium carbonate formed.

practice_mcq.q: The number of water molecules of crystallisation in washing soda is
practice_mcq.explanation: Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>·10H<sub>2</sub>O.

practice_mcq.q: Gypsum is heated at 373 K to obtain plaster of Paris. If it is heated to a much higher temperature, the product is
practice_mcq.explanation: Above 373 K gypsum loses all its water of crystallisation and forms anhydrous CaSO<sub>4</sub>, which does not set with water.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following salts is used for removing permanent hardness of water?
practice_mcq.explanation: Sodium carbonate (washing soda) precipitates dissolved calcium and magnesium ions as insoluble carbonates.

common_mistakes: Mixing up the two gas tests: hydrogen burns with a pop sound, carbon dioxide turns lime water milky. Writing the pop test for a carbonate reaction loses the full mark for the test.
Writing higher pH as stronger acid. Lower pH means higher H<sup>+</sup> concentration and a stronger acid; students reverse this in ordering questions like NCERT Q9.

Giving only one equation for the preparation of washing soda from baking soda. The examiner expects both the heating step (2NaHCO<sub>3</sub> → Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub>) and the recrystallisation step with ten water molecules.

Confusing baking soda (NaHCO<sub>3</sub>), soda ash (Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>) and washing soda (Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>·10H<sub>2</sub>O). Writing the wrong formula next to a correct use earns nothing for the formula.
Writing the plaster of Paris preparation without the temperature (373 K) or with the equation unbalanced. The 1½H<sub>2</sub>O on the right is the balancing detail examiners check.
Saying water is added to acid. It is always acid added to water, slowly and with stirring, because the process is exothermic; give both the reason and the consequence (splashing, cracking).

Describing the dry HCl activity without mentioning that the gas is dried in a calcium chloride guard tube and without the moist litmus observation, so the conclusion that acids need water is left unsupported.

In the chlor-alkali process, writing sodium metal as the cathode product (that is molten NaCl, Chapter 3) or swapping the electrodes. It is chlorine at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode, NaOH near the cathode.
Forgetting the subscript in H<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub>, or leaving equations unbalanced. Each unbalanced equation in a 3-mark question typically costs half a mark.
Classifying every metal-with-base reaction as giving hydrogen. NCERT says only some metals (zinc, for instance) react this way; do not generalise.
strategy:
This chapter is won on equations and on the four industrial salts. Start by writing every equation in the formula sheet from memory, balanced, on one page, and repeat that page daily until the week of the exam. There are about twenty; they cover nearly every 2- and 3-mark question the board has asked from this chapter.

Next, build one table for the salts: common name, chemical name, formula, preparation equation, two uses, and water of crystallisation. Fill it for sodium hydroxide, bleaching powder, baking soda, washing soda and plaster of Paris (with gypsum). Most 3-mark questions are a row of this table; most 5-mark questions are two or three rows compared.

Then rehearse the three NCERT activities that are always asked with a diagram or a description: zinc with dilute acid and the pop test, dry HCl with dry and moist litmus (with the guard tube), and heating copper sulphate crystals. For each, practise writing the setup, the observation and the conclusion in three sentences.

For pH, memorise the handful of numbers (5.6, 5.5, 7.0 to 7.8, and the approximate values of gastric juice, lemon juice, blood, milk of magnesia), the rule for pH of salts, and the reasoning answers on antacids, bee stings, tooth decay and soil. Case-based questions are built from exactly these paragraphs of the NCERT text.

Finally, solve all fifteen NCERT exercise questions and the in-text questions in writing at least once; several board questions are lifted from them with small changes. On the day, spend no more than 8 to 10 minutes on this chapter's questions; they are direct if you know the equations.
